title: The phone that ruled the world
hook: Four in ten phones on Earth are yours. Then a phone that is almost all screen arrives.

profit.label: Profit
profit.hint: Money the phone business makes today

future.label: Future
future.hint: How ready Nokia is for what comes next

intro.text: It is the end of 2007, and you run Nokia. This year, you sold 435 million phones, almost four in every ten phones sold on Earth, and India is one of your biggest markets. But in June, Apple started selling a phone that is almost all screen.

d1.title: The software question
d1.setup: Most smartphones in the world run your Symbian software, and you own about half of the company that makes it. But Symbian was built for phones with keypads, and now Google is bringing out Android, a new rival system for phones.
d1.question: What do you do with your smartphone software?
d1.advisor: Symbian earns us money today, and our engineers know it inside out. Starting again would be slow, costly and risky.

options.label: Buy all of Symbian and make it free for phone makers. It will cost millions.
options.outcome: You pay about €264 million for the rest of Symbian and plan to open its code to everyone. Now you own the world's most popular smartphone software, but it was built before the touchscreen, and making it feel modern is slow work.
options.why: Owning Symbian gave you control, but the software was built for an earlier kind of phone. Giving it away did not make it any better for touchscreens.
options.better: Keep Symbian for cheap phones, but start a new touch-first software team now and give it your best people.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you bought the past instead of building the future.

options.label: Keep Symbian and add touch step by step. It costs less, but progress will be slower.
options.outcome: Your engineers add touch to Symbian bit by bit. Each new phone is a little better than the last, but next to an iPhone it still feels old, and young buyers start to notice.
options.why: Small fixes to old software could not catch up with phones built for touch from day one.
options.better: Start a new touch-first software team now, even if it competes with Symbian.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you patched old software while the market moved on.

options.label: Start a separate touch-first software team. It will cost more and split your engineers.
options.outcome: A small team starts building new touch software while Symbian keeps paying the bills. It costs a lot and starts fights inside the company, but the team learns fast.
options.why: You paid to compete with your own best product before someone else did it for you.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you built your next software while the old one still made money.

text.text: By late 2010 your share of smartphones has fallen from almost half to under a third, and Apple now sells about one in six. You and Intel have joined your software into a new system called MeeGo, but no phone uses it yet. In September the board brings in a new boss from Microsoft. From here on, that boss is you.
By late 2010, iPhones and Android phones are everywhere, and your share of smartphones is falling fast. The board is losing patience, and it wants a new plan from you.
By late 2010 your new touch phones are in the shops, and they keep you in the race. But iPhones and Android phones are selling fast, and the board wants a plan for the next five years.

d2.title: Pick a platform

setup.text: Your own touch software works, but app makers are busy with Apple and Android. Samsung, LG and HTC all use Android. Microsoft wants a big partner for its own phone software, which very few people use.

Samsung, LG and HTC all use Google's Android. Microsoft wants a big partner for its phone software, which runs on only about 3 in every 100 smartphones. Your own new software, MeeGo, still isn't ready.

d2.question: Which software will power your smartphones?
d2.advisor: Whatever you choose, choose fast. Every month we wait, more buyers move on.

options.label: Bet everything on your own software. You keep control, but app makers may stay away.

outcome.text: Your own software keeps getting better, and reviewers love it. But app makers stay with Apple and Android, so your phones have beautiful screens and nearly empty app stores.
You keep full control, but the software arrives late, and few app makers want to build for one more system. Your phones look great, but their app stores are nearly empty.

options.why: Phones live or die by their apps. A fourth system, however good, struggled to win app makers.
options.better: Join the system app makers already support, and fight on hardware, price and shops.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you kept control, but your app store stayed empty.

options.label: Switch to Android like Samsung. You move faster, but Google sets the rules.
options.outcome: Your first Android phones arrive within a year. With huge factories and shops in every town, you sell them at every price, and buyers who left start to come back. But Google, not you, now sets the rules.
options.why: You joined the system buyers and app makers had already chosen, and fought with your real strengths: making phones and selling them everywhere.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you joined the winning system and fought on your strengths.

options.label: Partner with Microsoft on Windows Phone. You become its top partner, but few people use it yet.

outcome.text: In February 2011 you make Windows Phone your main smartphone software and push Symbian and MeeGo aside. Your share price falls almost a tenth that morning. You fear that with Android, Nokia would be just one of many phone makers, and the first Lumia phones arrive only in October.
Microsoft makes you its top partner, and you drop your own software. For most of a year you have no new smartphones to sell, and the people who were waiting for you buy an iPhone or an Android phone.

options.why: You tied your future to software that very few people used, and it took months before you had anything new to sell.
options.better: Choose the system buyers and app makers had already chosen, and fight on hardware, price and shops.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you bet on the software almost nobody was using.

d3.title: Hold on to India

setup.text: Your new smartphones are still months away, and India is slipping. You once had about 70% of India's phone market, but your share has fallen for nine quarters in a row. About half of Indian buyers want phones that take two SIM cards, and local brands like Micromax already sell them.

India is your biggest test. You once had about 70% of its phone market, but your share has fallen for nine quarters in a row. About half of Indian buyers want phones that take two SIM cards, and local brands like Micromax already sell them.

d3.question: How do you fight for India?
d3.advisor: Smartphones are where the world is going, but most Indian buyers today still count every rupee.

options.label: Focus on smartphones. You invest in the future but give up more of the cheap-phone market.
options.outcome: Samsung and local brands take the cheap and middle market, which is most of India. Your name is still in every shop, but fewer people walk out with your phone.
options.why: Most of India was buying cheap phones. Walking away from them handed your biggest market to rivals.
options.better: Give Indian buyers what they asked for: cheap phones with two SIM slots, sold through the shops you already had.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you chased rich buyers and lost India's millions.

options.label: Cut smartphone prices in India. You may win buyers, but you lose money on every phone.
options.outcome: Some buyers trade up to your smartphones, but most Indian buyers still want a cheap phone with two SIM slots. You win a little, and lose a lot of money on each phone.
options.why: Cheaper smartphones helped a little, but they were not what most Indian buyers were asking for.
options.better: Launch cheap dual-SIM phones, and give the shops that sell them a better margin.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you discounted the wrong phone.

options.label: Launch cheap dual-SIM phones and pay shops more. You protect share but stay in low-profit phones.

outcome.text: In June 2011 you launch dual-SIM phones in India. Later that year your new Asha phones sell for about Rs 3,000 to 8,000, and you give shops more margin. Your share of phones shipped still slips, from about a third to just over a fifth, but Nokia stays number one.
Cheap dual-SIM phones and better margins for shops slow the slide. Nokia stays the name most Indian shopkeepers push first.

options.why: You gave Indian buyers what they asked for and used your biggest strength, the shops that already sold your phones everywhere.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you listened to Indian buyers and used your shops.

text.text: It is 2013. Samsung now sells more phones than you, and Symbian has almost vanished. In 2012 your phone business sold €14.9 billion worth of phones but lost over €1 billion. Only one part of Nokia is doing well: Nokia Siemens Networks, which builds the equipment that mobile networks run on.

It is 2013. Your Android phones sell well, but the price war with Samsung never stops, and profits are thin. Meanwhile Nokia Siemens Networks, which builds the equipment that mobile networks run on, quietly makes good money.

It is 2013. Samsung now sells more phones than you, Windows phones are still rare, and your phone business loses money every quarter. Only one part of Nokia is doing well: Nokia Siemens Networks, which builds the equipment that mobile networks run on.

It is 2013. Your own phones still struggle to win app makers, and the losses are growing. Only one part of Nokia is doing well: Nokia Siemens Networks, which builds the equipment that mobile networks run on.

d4.title: The quiet winner
d4.setup: Nokia Siemens Networks made money in 2012 if you leave out one-off costs, while the phones lost money. Now your partner, Siemens, wants to sell its half of the networks business, and your cash is getting tight.
d4.question: What do you do with the networks business?
d4.advisor: Cash is short, and whatever we do with the networks business, we cannot easily undo it.

options.label: Sell your half too. The cash keeps the phones going, but the networks profit is gone.
options.outcome: You get a big cheque, but it disappears into a phone business that keeps losing money. Soon you have no strong business left to fall back on.
options.why: You sold the one business with a future to feed the one that was losing money.
options.better: Keep the profitable networks business, and own it fully if you can.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you sold your future to pay for your past.

options.label: Buy Siemens' half and own it all. You gain control but use much of your cash.

outcome.text: In July 2013 you agree to buy Siemens' half for €1.7 billion. Your shares rise more than 7% that day, but the deal uses up a lot of your cash.
You buy out Siemens and own the networks business fully. It uses up a lot of cash, but now all of its profit is yours.

options.why: You spent money to fully own the part of the company that made a profit and had a future, even while the famous part was in trouble.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you backed the quiet winner inside your own company.

options.label: List it on the stock market and keep a share. You raise cash but lose control.
options.outcome: You raise some cash and keep part of the profits, but you no longer control the business that could become Nokia's future.
options.why: Listing raised money, but it gave away control of your strongest business just when you needed it most.
options.better: Buy Siemens' half and own the profitable networks business fully.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you kept a slice of your future instead of all of it.

d5.title: The hardest call

setup.text: Your phone business is losing over €1 billion a year. Microsoft, your software partner, is ready to buy all of it.
Your Android phones hold their own, but Samsung is bigger and the price war never stops. Now a big tech company offers to buy your whole phone business.
Your phone business keeps losing money, and a big tech company offers to buy all of it.

d5.question: What do you do with the phone business that made Nokia famous?
d5.advisor: If we sell, Nokia stops making the phones the world knows us for. If we keep them, the losses go on. Neither choice is painless.

options.label: Refuse the deal and keep fighting. You keep the phone business but risk more losses.
options.outcome: You keep the famous phones, but the losses keep growing and eat up the cash your other businesses need.
options.why: You protected the name on the phone instead of the company behind it.
options.better: Sell while the business is still worth billions, and build on what makes money.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you held on to the past at any price.

options.label: Sell the phones and keep networks, maps and patents. You gain cash but leave phones behind.

outcome.text: In September 2013 you agree to sell the phone business to Microsoft for €5.44 billion, including money for a licence to your patents. About 32,000 staff move to Microsoft, and Nokia keeps its networks business, its HERE maps and its patents.
You sell the phones while they are still worth billions. It hurts to see your famous phones go, but Nokia now has cash and a clear road ahead.

options.why: You let go of what made Nokia famous to save what could keep Nokia alive, and you sold while the business was still worth a lot.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you let go of the famous part to save the company.

options.label: Refuse the deal and shrink the phone business. You cut losses but may lose more ground.
options.outcome: You close factories and sell only the phones that make money. The losses shrink, but so does Nokia, and the famous name slowly fades from the shops.
options.why: Shrinking slowed the bleeding, but it kept money and attention tied to a business that was fading.
options.better: Sell the phones while they are still worth billions, and put everything into networks.
options.takeaway: In 2013 you kept a smaller phone business alive, at a cost.

text.text: You sold the phones while they were still worth a lot, then built Nokia around the networks that carry the world's calls. The famous phones are gone, but Nokia comes out strong and ready for what comes next.
With early Android phones, shops in every town and the cheap phones India wanted, Nokia stays one of the world's top phone makers, and its networks business grows beside it.
You moved early and listened to buyers. Nokia stays one of the world's top phone makers, and its networks business grows beside it.

In April 2014 the sale to Microsoft closes. Nokia becomes mainly a networks company, with HERE maps and its patents, led by the head of its networks business. The phones that made it famous now belong to someone else, but Nokia itself survives.
The phones that made Nokia famous now belong to someone else. What is left is smaller, but it makes money, and Nokia itself survives.
Nokia still makes phones, but it is a smaller name every year. Its networks business is what keeps the company alive.

You held on to the past for too long, and you sold the one business that could have saved you. With the phones losing money and nothing strong to fall back on, Nokia becomes a story about how giants fall.
You held on to the past for too long. With the phones losing money and your cash running out, Nokia becomes a story people tell about how giants fall.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: The board has seen enough. After three costly calls, it asks someone else to steer Nokia through the storm.

realHistory: Nokia was the world's biggest phone maker, selling 40% of all phones at the end of 2007. Its share of smartphones fell fast, and in 2011 it chose Microsoft's Windows Phone instead of Android. Samsung passed it by the end of 2012. In 2013 Nokia bought full control of its profitable networks business and sold its phone business to Microsoft for €5.44 billion. From 2014 it lived on mainly as a networks company.
